title: Chapter 117 — The Coaching Craft
intro: A KPI tells you what happened. Coaching tells you why it happened and how to fix it. This chapter teaches you how to turn numbers into development — not punishment.

sections.title: KPIs Are Evidence — Not Judgment
sections.content:
A KPI is not the problem. A KPI is evidence that points toward a problem.

The manager's job is not to react to the number. The manager's job is to discover why the number exists.

Example: two salespeople. Salesperson A has a 15 percent closing ratio. Salesperson B has a 40 percent closing ratio. The question is not 'why is one good and one bad?' The question is 'what is creating the difference?'

Everything else starts there. If you skip this step — if you go straight to lecturing the 15 percent person about their numbers — you are guessing at the solution. And guessing at solutions is the same mistake you teach salespeople to avoid with customers.

sections.title: Observe Before You Coach
sections.content:
When I see someone with a significantly lower closing percentage than the rest of the team, I do not immediately assume they are a poor salesperson.

Instead, I start observing. I listen. I watch customer interactions. I review their sales process. I look for patterns.

Coaching should be based on evidence, not assumptions.

Maybe the problem is their presentation. Maybe it is how they handle objections. Maybe it is the product tour they are using. Maybe it is something you would never guess from a spreadsheet — they are not connecting with customers because their energy is off, or they are talking too much, or they are skipping discovery.

You will never know from a dashboard. You have to be on the floor.

sections.title: Managers Belong on the Floor
sections.content:
One of the biggest mistakes retailers make is burying managers in paperwork. Reports. Emails. Schedules. Operational tasks. All of those matter.

But if sales stop, none of the rest matters.

Sales create the revenue that allows every other department to exist. A sales manager's primary responsibility is developing salespeople. That requires spending time on the sales floor — not in the office.

I think this is one of the most important things I can say to anyone in a leadership role in retail: if you are spending more time on paperwork than on coaching, your priorities are backwards. Being a pure salesman and thinking about operations later — your goal when you walk into the store is first to make sure the presentation value is right, then get on the floor and work with your people.

sections.title: The Individual Coaching Checklist
sections.content:
Once you have observed and identified the gap, focus your coaching on the specific step that is breaking down. Run through the 10 Steps:

Step 1 — Engagement: are they greeting effectively or letting customers wander?
Step 2 — Rapport: are they building connection or jumping straight to product?
Step 3 — Discovery: are they asking enough questions or assuming what the customer wants?
Step 4 — Needs Assessment: do they understand the functional requirements?
Step 5 — Wants Assessment: do they uncover lifestyle and emotional drivers?
Step 6 — Product Recommendation: are they recommending the right product — or the easiest one?
Step 7 — Presentation: are they demonstrating with purpose or just listing features?
Step 8 — Objection Handling: are they investigating concerns or arguing?
Step 9 — Closing: are they asking directly for the sale?
Step 10 — Follow-up: are they building a pipeline or forgetting the customer the moment they leave?

The KPI identifies where to investigate. Observation determines what to coach.

sections.title: Raise the Middle
sections.content:
Every sales team has top performers, middle performers, and lower performers. Most managers spend all their time with the bottom performers.

The greatest opportunity often lies in the middle.

Example: your top performer does $200,000 a month. Your middle does $150,000. Your bottom does $100,000. The objective is not necessarily turning everyone into the top performer. It is raising the average.

Move the middle from $150,000 to $160,000. Then $170,000. Then $180,000. Small improvements across multiple people create larger business gains than relying on one superstar.

The goal is not to create one exceptional salesperson. The goal is to improve the entire team's average performance. Great managers build stronger teams. Weak managers rely on stronger individuals.

sections.title: Coach the Process — Not the Outcome
sections.content:
When you coach, never say 'your closing ratio is too low — close more deals.' That is not coaching. That is just restating the problem.

Instead, pick one specific behavior and work on it.

'I noticed you are skipping the demo on about half your customers. Let us work on that this week. I want you to do a full product demonstration with every customer — even when you think you already know the right product.'

That is actionable. That gives the salesperson something they can actually change tomorrow. If the demo improves and closing follows, you have confirmed the diagnosis. If it does not, you look at the next step.

Coaching is iterative. You do not fix everything at once. You fix one thing, observe, adjust, and fix the next thing.

sections.title: The Culture Check
sections.content:
Before coaching any individual, evaluate whether the problem is personal or cultural.

Signs of a cultural problem: losing sales is considered normal. Average performance is accepted. Nobody is held accountable. Coaching is inconsistent. Winning is not celebrated. Improvement is not expected.

If the entire team is underperforming, coaching one person will not fix it. You need to address the culture — the expectations, the accountability, the standards, and the environment. Culture always influences KPIs. A single salesperson performing below average might have a skills gap. An entire team performing below average has a leadership gap.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating your own coaching effectiveness, ask:

Are you observing salespeople on the floor — or just reading their numbers from the office?
Are you coaching specific behaviors — or just telling people to sell more?
Are you spending time with middle performers — or only the bottom?
Are you improving the team average — or relying on one or two stars?
Are you using KPIs as coaching tools — or as punishment?
Do your people trust that coaching is meant to help them — or are they afraid of it?

A KPI tells you what happened. Coaching tells you why it happened and how to improve it. That is the difference between a scorekeeper and a leader.
